one_liner: Rust Starknet library whose starknet-crypto Pedersen hash, compiled to WebAssembly, ran 6.88x faster than pure-JS micro-starknet in Node.js (2022).
what_it_does: starknet-rs is a Rust workspace for Starknet clients (providers, accounts, contracts, signers); the measured part is its low-level starknet-crypto crate, which exposes pedersen_hash(&Felt, &Felt) -> Felt alongside Poseidon, ECDSA sign/verify/recover and RFC 6979. To use it from JavaScript you build starknet-crypto for wasm32 and write wasm-bindgen glue yourself (examples/starknet-wasm shows the pattern with wasm-pack; it exports only get_public_key). It is not a drop-in for micro-starknet/scure-starknet, whose pedersen() takes hex strings, bigints or numbers and returns a hex string.
how_it_is_fast: Pedersen hash here is a fixed-base subset sum over four Stark-curve points; the crate precomputes 4-bit lookup tables (15 affine multiples per 4-bit chunk, 62 chunks for the low 248 bits plus one for the top 4 bits of each input) and adds one table point per non-zero nibble with mixed projective-affine addition, so a hash costs about 120 point additions and one inversion. The 2022 code that was benchmarked (rev 76e32ef, from PR #245) ported this table from eqlabs/pathfinder on top of ark-ff 0.3 Montgomery arithmetic; current releases (checked at 0.7.4 and 0.8.1) delegate pedersen_hash to starknet-types-core, which calls lambdaworks' PedersenStarkCurve, a port of the same 4-bit table. The JavaScript baseline at the pinned commit walks all 252 bits of each input and does one BigInt Jacobian addition per set bit (its windowed variant is commented out), so the ratio mixes algorithm and runtime.
when_to_use: Rust services, indexers or wallets that compute many Starknet Pedersen hashes (contract addresses, Merkle-Patricia nodes, hash chains) natively: 13 us per hash on an Apple M3 Max per the crate README.

Browser or Node.js code that hashes in bulk and can ship a wasm module: about 65 us per hash under wasmtime on the M3 Max, against 883 us per hash for scure-starknet in JS on an Apple M4 (different machines and runtimes, so only a rough gap).
Projects already in Rust that want one dependency covering Pedersen, Poseidon, ECDSA and RFC 6979 for the Stark curve, with no_std support.
When the hash path's 100 KB-plus lookup table in the binary is acceptable; otherwise the pedersen_no_lookup feature trades about 10x speed for size.
when_not_to_use: Signing with secret keys in hostile environments: the README states starknet-crypto has no constant-time guarantees and is not audited, while scure-starknet (the renamed micro-starknet) reports an audit funded by StarkWare.
Small JS apps that hash a handful of values: wasm instantiation, binary size of the lookup table and the glue code outweigh a ~1 ms per-hash saving.
When you need a ready-made npm package: starknet-rs ships no wasm npm build of starknet-crypto; you write and maintain the wasm-bindgen wrapper.
When you rely on the 6.88x figure for capacity planning: it was measured on 2022 code that has since been replaced by the lambdaworks implementation, against a JS version that has also changed.
Projects that need a stable API: the README calls the library experimental with breaking changes before 1.0 (starknet-crypto went 0.7 to 0.8 in August 2025).

integration.dependencies: starknet-crypto 0.8.1: starknet-types-core 0.2 (lambdaworks-math and lambdaworks-crypto), starknet-curve, crypto-bigint, hmac, sha2, rfc6979, num-bigint/num-integer/num-traits, zeroize; for JS use add wasm-bindgen (and wasm-pack) yourself
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 2021 edition; no rust-version (MSRV) declared in Cargo.toml
integration.platforms: any Rust target; no_std with optional alloc; wasm32 (wasm32-wasi in the benchmark, wasm32-unknown-unknown via wasm-bindgen in the example)
integration.thread_safety: pedersen_hash is a pure function over immutable static tables; PedersenHasher is a plain owned struct; not otherwise documented

gotchas: Harness asymmetry: the JS baseline at micro-starknet a1e7fa0 is a bit-serial subset sum (252 iterations per input, one BigInt Jacobian add per set bit, plus a per-step point-equality check), its windowed path commented out, while starknet-rs uses a 4-bit lookup table with mixed additions; part of the 6.88x is the table algorithm, which a JS port could also use, not WebAssembly versus JS.

The benchmarked code no longer ships: rev 76e32ef used starknet-ff (ark-ff 0.3) with a codegen lookup_table!(4); starknet-crypto 0.7.4 and 0.8.1 call starknet_types_core::hash::Pedersen, i.e. lambdaworks, so the 2022 numbers describe a predecessor implementation.

WebAssembly runs about 7x slower than native here (228.67 us wasm vs 31.99 us native on the same Ryzen 9 5950X in 2022; 64.96 vs 13.02 us on the M3 Max now); issue #241 reporting the gap was closed 'not planned' in July 2023, so do not expect native speed in the browser.
The benchmark linked only starknet-crypto and starknet-ff, not the whole starknet crate; pulling starknet (providers, reqwest, serde) into a wasm module is a separate and much larger build.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Among the catalogued wasm libraries the closest analogues are bls-eth-wasm and tiny-secp256k1, which replace pure-JS elliptic-curve code for BLS12-381 and secp256k1; pick starknet-crypto only when the curve is the Stark curve and the hash is Starknet Pedersen, since none of the siblings implement it. For general-purpose hashes in the browser, hash-wasm is the packaged choice.
verified_claims_summary: In xJonathanLEI/pedersen-bench (November 2022), one pedersen_hash on fixed inputs took 228.67 us for starknet-crypto rev 76e32ef built with cargo wasi --release and run by criterion 0.4 under wasmer-js 0.4.1 on Node.js v18.12.1, against a 1.573 ms benchmark.js mean for micro-starknet a1e7fa0 in the same Node.js, on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X with Ubuntu 20.04.5 (6.88x); the same repo's native table shows starknet-rs 1.15x slower than pathfinder.
status_note: Maintained but slowing (last commit 2025-11-09, starknet-crypto 0.8.1 released August 2025, 4.8 million crates.io downloads), dual MIT/Apache-2.0 and easy to depend on, but the 2022 benchmark measured code that has since been replaced by the lambdaworks implementation, so the ratio is stale and first-party.
